1091.event_title: Ernest Hemingway and the nurse Agnes von Kurowsky
1091.place: Milan, Italy, and Oak Park, Illinois, United States
1091.event: After the young Ernest Hemingway was wounded on the Italian front in July 1918, he was treated at the American Red Cross hospital in Milan, where he fell in love with the nurse Agnes von Kurowsky. They exchanged daily notes and became engaged. In March 1919, after he had returned home to Oak Park, she ended the engagement by letter, and the rejection hurt him deeply.
1091.explanation: The romance stayed with Hemingway and fed into his later fiction, including A Very Short Story and A Farewell to Arms.
1091.tie_back: The kural says one look of the beloved brings the ache of love and another is its medicine; for Hemingway the same woman was the nurse who cared for him and the source of his heartache.
1091._accuracy_note: The beloved as both healer and cause of pain fits well, but the kural speaks of two looks at one moment, and here the healing and the hurt came months apart.

1092.event_title: Clara Wieck and Robert Schumann's secret engagement
1092.event: The pianist Clara Wieck and the composer Robert Schumann fell in love, but her father, Friedrich Wieck, forbade contact when she was sixteen and refused Robert's formal request to marry her. The couple kept their engagement secret and finally took the matter to court, which granted permission in 1840. They married on 12 September 1840.
1092.explanation: Their love, carried on in secret against fierce opposition, became one of the best-known partnerships in the history of music.
1092.tie_back: The kural prizes the glance a lover steals when no one is looking; for years Clara and Robert's love could live only in such hidden moments and secret contact.
1092._accuracy_note: Shows secret love that had to be carried on by stealth, but the kural's specific image of a stolen glance is not documented for this couple.

1093.event_title: Queen Victoria proposes to Prince Albert
1093.event: Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha arrived at Windsor in October 1839, and five days later, on 15 October, Queen Victoria proposed to him. As the reigning monarch she could not traditionally be proposed to, so she had to take the first step. They married at the Chapel Royal, St James's Palace, on 10 February 1840.
1093.explanation: Their marriage became one of the most famous royal love matches, and Victoria's journal records her joy at being loved.
1093.tie_back: The kural describes the moment the beloved shows her consent, which waters the growing plant of love; Victoria herself gave that sign, and the courtship at once became a marriage.
1093._accuracy_note: A clear moment of a woman signalling her love and consent, though Victoria did it in words, not with the bowed head of the kural.

1094.event_title: Alexander Graham Bell and Mabel Hubbard
1094.place: Boston and Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States
1094.event: Mabel Hubbard, who had been left deaf by scarlet fever at the age of five and had learned to lip-read, met Alexander Graham Bell in 1873 when she came to him to improve her speech. Her journal records that at first she both did and did not like him. Her feelings grew into admiration and love; they became engaged in 1875 and married on 11 July 1877 in Cambridge, Massachusetts.
1094.explanation: Their long marriage, carried on through speech, lip-reading and letters, was a lifelong partnership.
1094.tie_back: The kural pictures a young woman whose love shows only in shy, hidden ways at first; Mabel's early mixed feelings slowly gave way to open love.
1094._accuracy_note: Shows love that began hesitantly, but there is no record of the specific shy looking-away and hidden smile the kural describes.

1095.event_title: Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa and her famous smile
1095.place: Florence, Italy (now in the Louvre, Paris)
1095.event: Leonardo da Vinci began the portrait known as the Mona Lisa in Florence around 1503 and worked on it for years. The sitter is traditionally identified as Lisa Gherardini, wife of the merchant Francesco del Giocondo. Her slight, enigmatic smile, painted with soft sfumato shading, has fascinated viewers for centuries.
1095.explanation: The quiet, half-hidden smile has made it probably the most famous painting in the world.
1095.tie_back: The kural describes a girl who does not look straight at her lover yet smiles quietly to herself; the Mona Lisa's restrained, private smile is the best-known image of such a look.
1095._accuracy_note: Captures a quiet private smile, but the painting is not a scene of courtship, and this artwork also appears in chapter 109.

1096.event_title: Robert Browning's first letter to Elizabeth Barrett
1096.event: Elizabeth Barrett, an admired poet who was very ill and mostly confined to her room at 50 Wimpole Street, had praised Robert Browning's work. On 10 January 1845 Browning, who had never met her, wrote to tell her that he loved her verses with all his heart. They first met on 20 May 1845, and on 12 September 1846 they married at St Marylebone Church.
1096.explanation: Their correspondence, begun between strangers, became one of the great love stories of English literature.
1096.tie_back: The kural says that even when people speak as if they were strangers, their real meaning is quickly understood; a letter from one stranger to another carried a meaning both soon recognised as love.
1096._accuracy_note: A good fit for meaning understood beneath a stranger's words, though the kural pictures lovers pretending distance, not genuine strangers.

1097.event_title: John Adams lists Abigail Smith's faults
1097.place: Braintree and Weymouth, Massachusetts, British America
1097.event: During their courtship, John Adams, signing himself Lysander, wrote to Abigail Smith listing her supposed faults in a mock-serious voice: she did not play cards, had never learned to sing, sat with her legs crossed, and walked with her toes turned in. Abigail, signing herself Diana, replied two days later in the same teasing spirit, accepting some faults and rejecting others. They married in October 1764.
1097.explanation: The exchange shows the playful affection that ran through one of the most famous marriages in American history.
1097.tie_back: The kural says small sharp words with no anger in them are a sign of hidden love; John's list of faults and Abigail's witty reply were exactly that.
1097._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's affectionate sharp words, though the kural also mentions hostile-seeming looks, which are not recorded here.

1098.event: Samuel Clemens (Mark Twain) proposed to Olivia Langdon in 1868, soon after meeting her, and she refused. He kept writing to her for about seventeen months, sending more than 180 letters, and kept visiting Elmira. They became engaged in February 1869 and married at the Langdon home in Elmira on 2 February 1870.
1098.explanation: Their marriage lasted until Olivia's death and was central to Twain's life and work.
1098.tie_back: The kural's lover looks at his beloved imploringly until she softens; Twain's long, pleading courtship slowly turned Olivia's refusal into acceptance.
1098._accuracy_note: A strong match for a pleading lover who wins the beloved's softening, though the kural describes a single smiling moment rather than a long courtship.

1099.event_title: Tchaikovsky and Nadezhda von Meck agree never to meet
1099.event: The wealthy widow Nadezhda von Meck became the patron of the composer Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky after first writing to him in December 1876, and she later paid him an allowance that let him leave teaching and compose full time. For about fourteen years they exchanged more than 1,200 letters, yet by her wish they agreed never to meet in person. She ended the relationship and the allowance in 1890.
1099.explanation: Their friendship is one of the most famous relationships in music history, intimate on paper yet kept at a distance in person.
1099.tie_back: The kural says that keeping up the appearance of strangers is something only those who are close do; Tchaikovsky and von Meck kept apart as strangers in person while sharing deep intimacy in letters.
1099._accuracy_note: Shows a close bond kept outwardly distant, but the relationship was not a romantic love affair, which is what the kural describes.

1100.place: Thebes (Valley of the Kings), Egypt; now in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo
1100.event: Among the treasures found in the antechamber of Tutankhamun's tomb was a throne covered in gold and inlaid with silver, semi-precious stones and glass paste. Its back panel shows the young king seated and his queen, Ankhesenamun, facing him and reaching out to touch his shoulder, beneath the spreading rays of the sun. Howard Carter called it the most beautiful thing yet found in Egypt.
1100.explanation: The scene is one of the most famous images of tenderness between a husband and wife to survive from the ancient world.
1100.tie_back: The kural says that when two lovers' looks meet, words are useless; the throne shows king and queen facing each other in a wordless moment of affection.
1100._accuracy_note: Shows wordless affection between a couple, but it is an artwork whose meaning is courtly and religious as much as personal, and the meeting of eyes is not described by the sources.
